conditions.name: Common cold (upper respiratory tract infection)

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

conditions.summary: A self-limiting viral infection of the nose and throat. Blocked and runny nose, sneezing, mild sore throat, and a cough that appears a few days in.

triage.action: Call emergency services or go to an emergency department now

exam.positive: Persistence beyond 12 weeks is the defining feature separating this from acute sinusitis, which settles within a few weeks
Reduced or lost smell is a genuine, common feature of chronic disease, more so than in a typical acute episode

exam.step: Check whether symptoms are one-sided, or whether there is blood-stained discharge or any visual/neurological symptom
exam.positive: Any of these should prompt imaging to exclude a structural or malignant cause rather than assuming simple chronic sinusitis

conditions.name: Chronic rhinosinusitis

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: Nasal blockage, thick nasal discharge, facial pressure/pain and reduced sense of smell, persisting beyond 12 weeks -- distinct from ordinary acute sinusitis, which settles much sooner. Air pollution and the high ambient allergen/dust load in many Indian cities are relevant chronic drivers worth asking about alongside standard advice. Unilateral symptoms with blood-stained discharge, or visual/neurological symptoms, should prompt imaging to exclude a structural or malignant cause rather than assuming simple chronic sinusitis.
workup: CT sinuses if surgery being considered or diagnosis unclear
Allergy testing if an allergic component is suspected
Saline irrigation and intranasal corticosteroid are first-line and often very effective
Longer antibiotic courses or oral steroids for flares
Endoscopic sinus surgery for refractory disease/nasal polyps

exam.step: Ask exactly how the bleeding was managed and for how long
exam.positive: Correctly applied pressure (soft part of the nose, 15-20 minutes, leaning forward, not lying back) fails to stop far less often than incorrectly applied pressure

exam.step: Ask about blood-thinning medication and high blood pressure
exam.positive: Both are recognised contributing factors and change how aggressively to investigate and manage recurrent bleeds

exam.step: Ask whether blood is also being felt/tasted at the back of the throat despite front-of-nose pressure
exam.positive: Suggests posterior epistaxis -- needs urgent ENT assessment, not standard first aid alone

labs.test: Clinical assessment and blood pressure check
labs.confirms: Sufficient for a single, minor, self-limiting bleed

labs.test: Full blood count and clotting screen
labs.confirms: Reserved for recurrent, severe, or anticoagulant-related bleeding

conditions.name: Epistaxis (nosebleed)

triage.label: Self-care
triage.action: This can usually be managed at home

conditions.summary: Bleeding from the nose, most commonly from Little's area at the front of the septum -- often triggered by dry air, nose picking/trauma, or in the context of high blood pressure or blood-thinning medication. Genuinely common, especially in the dry season, and highly amenable to clear first-aid self-care. Heavy, prolonged bleeding not controlled by 15-20 minutes of correct first-aid pressure, or bleeding from the back of the nose (posterior epistaxis), needs urgent ENT assessment.
workup: Full blood count and clotting if recurrent, severe, or on blood thinners
Firm continuous pressure on the soft part of the nose for a full 15-20 minutes, leaning forward
Nasal cautery or packing if first aid fails
Treat underlying high blood pressure or a clotting problem if found

redFlags.label: Possible sepsis
redFlags.message: A fever together with confusion, very fast breathing, mottled skin or a collapsing blood pressure can mean infection is affecting the whole body.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Do not wait to see whether it settles.

redFlags.label: Rash that does not fade under pressure
redFlags.message: Spots that stay visible when a glass is pressed on them, alongside feeling unwell, can be a sign of bacteria in the bloodstream.

redFlags.label: Possible severe allergic reaction
redFlags.message: Swelling of the throat or tongue with difficulty breathing after a food, sting, or medicine can close the airway within minutes.
redFlags.action: Use an adrenaline auto-injector if you have one, then call emergency services.

redFlags.label: Reduced consciousness
redFlags.message: Being difficult to rouse, or drifting in and out of awareness, always needs immediate assessment whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Place the person on their side if unresponsive.

redFlags.label: Possible stroke
redFlags.message: Sudden facial drooping, arm weakness or difficulty speaking is a stroke until proven otherwise. Treatment works only within a few hours.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now and note the exact time symptoms began.

redFlags.label: Seizure
redFlags.message: A first seizure needs assessment to find the cause and to advise on driving and safety.
redFlags.action: Seek urgent assessment today. Call emergency services if the seizure lasted over five minutes or a second one followed.

redFlags.label: Significant gastrointestinal bleeding
redFlags.message: Vomiting blood, or passing black tarry stools, means bleeding inside the digestive tract.
redFlags.action: Go to an emergency department now.

redFlags.label: New jaundice
redFlags.message: Yellowing of the skin or eyes always needs blood tests to find out why.

redFlags.label: Sudden loss of vision
redFlags.message: Sight lost suddenly in one or both eyes needs assessment the same hour, whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Go to an eye emergency department now.

redFlags.label: Thoughts of self-harm
redFlags.message: Thoughts of harming yourself or of being better off dead deserve help today. You do not have to be in crisis to reach out.
redFlags.action: Contact your doctor, a crisis line, or go to an emergency department now. If you are in immediate danger, call emergency services.

redFlags.label: New confusion coming on over hours or days
redFlags.message: Confusion that has come on over hours or days, or that comes and goes through the day, is delirium until proven otherwise. It is caused by something else -- an infection, a drug, pain, retention -- and that cause needs finding today.
redFlags.action: Seek same-day medical assessment. Take a list of all medications. Call emergency services if they are drowsy, feverish or cannot be roused properly.

disclaimer: This tool provides information about possible causes of symptoms. It is not a diagnosis and it cannot examine you. It does not replace assessment by a qualified clinician. If you feel very unwell, or your symptoms are getting rapidly worse, seek medical help immediately regardless of what this tool says.
